title: All shall be well
hookLine: Julian heard: all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well (Revelations 27)
carry: a love bigger than the hurt

cards: It's a question that tends to come at night, after bad news. A diagnosis. A child in trouble.
A headline you can't stop thinking about. If God is good, why is there so much wrong in the world? Why didn't God just prevent it?
Julian of Norwich asked exactly that, not as a debate but in prayer. She wondered why, in God's great wisdom, sin hadn't simply been stopped at the start.
The answer she received has traveled a long way from her small room. Today: behovely.

teach.b: It's in chapter twenty-seven of her book. Julian thinks that if only there had never been sin, everything would have been fine. Why allow it?
First, a strange phrase: sin is behovely, an old word meaning something like fitting, or bound to be. Scholars still discuss exactly what she meant.

Then, in Grace Warrack's 1901 version, the well-known words: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Notice what the answer doesn't do. It doesn't explain the suffering.
It doesn't say the pain isn't real, or that it's secretly good. Julian says plainly she didn't understand how it could be true. She saw the evil in the world clearly.

Later she even says God will do a great deed at the end of time, and that we can't know now what it is or how it will make everything well. So this isn't optimism, which says things will probably work out.
As she hears it, even the things that won't work out are held inside a love bigger than they are.
And it comes in three beats, like a heartbeat: all shall be well; and all shall be well; and all manner of thing, every kind of thing, shall be well. Centuries later, the poet T. S.
Eliot wove her words into his poem Little Gidding. Look back at this week: Hildegard's greening, Bernard's four loves, Francis's family of creatures, the cloud, Julian's cell, her hazelnut.
Each, in a different way, kept coming back to love.

how: Some Christians repeat Julian's words in times of grief or fear, and her line is read at funerals, printed on cards, and prayed slowly as a single sentence.

p: at the end, not known now

s: all shall be well means nothing bad is really happening
Julian saw evil clearly; the promise sits beside the pain, not instead of it.
Julian said she didn't understand how it could be true
she held the promise without a full explanation.
a modern poet wove her words into a well-known poem

games.q: you're Julian. you've asked why God didn't simply prevent sin. what kind of answer comes?
o: a promise: all shall be well.
games.why: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." a promise, not an explanation.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that is not well right now, and hold it honestly, without pushing it away. Then say Julian's words slowly, aloud or silently: all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.
Don't force the feeling; let the words sit next to the thing that hurts.

wordCard.voice: Behovely. Julian's strange old word for sin: fitting, or bound to be, spoken just before the promise that all shall be well.

carryVoice: Your line: a love bigger than the hurt. Not optimism; held in love. A week done, and day two hundred seventy-three.

sources.ref: Julian of Norwich, Revelations of Divine Love, ch. 27
